9.12 Support-data agent controls
A support-data query can request an exact count, examples, or a summary of support requests. Each needs a different result check. The Bitext case from Section 9.2 combines a router, typed dataset tools, graph state, and answer-and-policy validation around the model’s proposed actions. The application records each route, call, observation, and stop reason so failures can be located.
The dataset contains synthetic labeled customer-support requests, not a record of actual customers’ activity. Each row carries request text and an intent label such as get_refund. An exact-label count has a deterministic expected result once the dataset version and authorized rows are fixed. Natural-language routing and summaries still need their own tests and scoring criteria.
The router classifies structured, unstructured, or out-of-scope requests before tool selection. Structured questions use deterministic dataset tools for categories, filtering, counts, examples, and distributions. Unstructured questions use selected rows as evidence for summarization. Out-of-scope questions receive a clear decline with the supported scope and next available route.
Suppose an authorized dataset version contains 27 rows labelled get_refund. This illustrative count is not a measured count of the full Bitext dataset. For How many refund requests are in the dataset?, the example first calls filter_by_intent(intent='get_refund', limit=20). The tool stores the complete filtered IDs and returns {"row_ref": ..., "preview": [...]}. The preview contains at most 20 rows. The next call, count_rows(rows=row_ref), checks the caller and dataset version and returns {"count": 27, "dataset_version": ..., "intent": "get_refund"}. It counts stored IDs rather than preview rows. The model reports the tool’s count instead of computing it. An answer should identify its authorized dataset scope so that 27 is not mistaken for a global count.
A maximum iteration limit returns a fallback if no supported answer is produced. The command-line interface exposes tool calls, results, and stop reasons for debugging without requiring private model reasoning. A durable checkpointer restores session state after restart. A separate profile of selected user facts is an optional feature with its own update and deletion policy in Chapter 11. The source case also exposes tools through FastMCP, a Python library for creating shared tool servers. Sections 9.7–9.8 explain Model Context Protocol (MCP), the server connection, and permissions. Hosting a tool remotely is not required for the action loop itself.

Chapter conclusion
The model proposes actions. Application code checks and executes them, manages session state and budgets, and stops the loop. Code execution, remote tools, and retrieval retries need checks suited to their effects. Repeated trials test whether outcomes and policy checks pass consistently. Chapter 10 builds on this execution layer to plan remaining work and coordinate agent loops.

9  Controlled tool use by agents

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
10.1 Choosing a planning strategy
A tool-using agent can choose one action after each observation, as Chapter 9 showed. Some tasks also need a visible account of the work still to do: which sources remain to be checked, which results depend on others, and which steps can run together. Planning makes that work inspectable before or during execution. Dividing it among agents adds a further choice about who acts and how control returns.
Planning and coordination answer different questions. A plan describes proposed work and dependencies. Coordination assigns work, transfers the needed context, and checks returned results. Either still uses the execution checks, permissions, budgets, and stopping rules from Chapter 9.
The first choice is whether the next useful step can be identified before a tool returns. ReAct in Section 9.3 chooses again from each observation. An explicit plan is useful when remaining work needs review, dependent steps need ordering, or independent work could overlap.
A planner is the model or software component that proposes steps and their order from a goal and the available state. The application checks the proposed work before execution. A planning policy is the rule or model instruction used to make those choices.
The following approaches organize different parts of that work:
Reflexion provides feedback between attempts rather than a particular way to order tasks.5 CodeAct, taught in Section 9.6, supplies an action format: executable code. These techniques can complement a planning method. They are not interchangeable planners.
The comparison table includes the ReAct baseline and these related techniques. It distinguishes their roles, task fit, and cost or failure risk. Sections 10.2–10.6 develop the planning and feedback mechanisms; Sections 10.7–10.8 explain distributing work among agent loops.
The choice follows the task. Unknown next actions favor observation-driven decisions. Predictable work can use an upfront plan. Dependencies determine which calls must wait, while measured execution cost determines whether parallel scheduling is worthwhile. A plan that is easy to inspect can still be wrong, incomplete, or outside the caller’s permissions.

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
Plan-and-Execute writes an initial plan, then carries out its steps. Plan-and-Solve is a related prompting method that asks a model to plan and solve a reasoning problem within generated text.1
ReWOO writes tool instructions ahead of observations and uses variables to refer to results that will arrive later.2
Plan-and-Act separates high-level planning from concrete environment actions. Its replanning variant revises the remaining plan after observations.3
LLMCompiler organizes function calls as a dependency graph and dispatches ready work in parallel.4






Table 10.1: Planning, feedback, and action methods solve different parts of the agent’s task.











Method
Control structure
Best fit
Primary cost or risk




ReAct
One action after each observation
Exploratory tasks and uncertain scope
Sequential latency, token use, and loop risk


Plan-and-Execute
Create a full plan, then execute its steps
Stable tasks where the plan can be reviewed before action
Stale plans when observations invalidate later steps


Plan-and-Solve
Prompt a reasoning plan, solve it, then extract an answer
Supplied-fact problems with dependent reasoning steps
Missing or incorrect reasoning; no access to missing facts


ReWOO
Create variable-linked tool work before observations return
Tasks whose tool sequence can be planned before observations
Unexpected observations can invalidate a fixed plan; revising the tool plan needs an added control path


Reflexion
Generate and store a reflection from feedback between attempts

Plan-and-Act
Separate high-level planning from execution, optionally replan from observations
Clear phases whose details change with observations
Replanning call cost and errors in revised plans


LLMCompiler
Stream a dependency graph and dispatch ready nodes
Independent subtasks with a merge step
Dependency correctness and harder traces


CodeAct
Emit executable code as the action
Loops, data transformation, and library composition
Untrusted-code execution requires isolation

10  Planning and coordinating agents

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
10.2 Plan-and-Execute and Plan-and-Solve
Suppose a user asks an application to compare the return windows for headphones and monitors. Both policy sources are available, and the required product categories are known. The application can propose the work before retrieving either policy: find the two sources, extract the relevant conditions, compare the windows, and return an answer with citations.
In a Plan-and-Execute design, planning produces a list of proposed steps. The application checks required inputs, tool availability, permissions, and dependencies. An executor then runs permitted steps and stores each result. A later step receives the earlier results it needs. Completion requires the requested answer and its policy checks, not just an empty work list.
For this illustrative policy comparison, one execution is:

The planner proposes finding the headphone and monitor policies, then comparing their conditions and deadlines.
The application permits the two read operations. Each returns an approved passage with a source reference.
An extraction step returns the product, deadline, and conditions from each passage.
The comparison step checks that the conditions match the question and drafts the answer. Final validation checks both product coverage and citation support.

The plan makes missing work visible before execution. It does not make the passages relevant or the extraction correct. An empty search result blocks comparison. If a policy introduces an unforeseen condition, the application needs clarification, a revised plan, or a fallback rather than continuing with the original assumptions. Section 10.4 develops that revision path. An upfront plan fits predictable work, but can waste planning effort when the first observation changes the task.
Plan-and-Solve addresses a smaller problem: a model can omit a needed reasoning step even when the prompt supplies all the facts. Wang et al. ask the model to devise a plan and carry out its reasoning. Their evaluation then uses another prompt to extract the answer. PS+ adds guidance about relevant variables and intermediate calculations to address calculation errors as well as missing steps.6 This is prompt-based reasoning, not a tool executor or a saved application work queue.

Example: A plan within a reasoning prompt
Suppose a prompt says that three cartons each contain 12 headphones and that five headphones are removed. It asks how many remain. The plan first finds the total, 3 × 12 = 36, then subtracts the removed units, 36 − 5 = 31. The second calculation depends on the first. Skipping the multiplication would use the stock in one carton rather than all three.
Result: The answer is 31 headphones. The model used the supplied facts; no inventory service was called or stock changed. Application code can check the arithmetic directly. This illustrates the missing-step problem, not a measured benefit of the prompt.

A request that needs current or private policy text still needs a permitted way to obtain it. Planning instructions alone do not supply missing facts. The paper’s reasoning-task results therefore do not establish tool-use reliability. For an application, the relevant comparison is whether plan-first reasoning or execution improves checked answers enough to justify its extra work.

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
section: 10.3 ReWOO: tool plans with output variables
text:
10.3 ReWOO: tool plans with output variables
An upfront plan can know that a document must be read without knowing its identifier yet. ReWOO represents that missing value with an evidence variable. Its planner writes the tool work before seeing observations, workers obtain the results, and a solver combines the plan and evidence into an answer.7
A later tool instruction can refer to an earlier variable. The application substitutes the actual result when it becomes available. That dependency does not require another planner call merely to copy a returned value into the next tool’s argument. It also does not make the two calls independent or automatically parallel.
For the same policy comparison, suppose the search tool returns a policy reference and a separate read tool returns its text. The following is a plan trace, not an executable program:

The planner writes E1 = search_policy("headphones") and E2 = read_policy(E1.policy_ref).
It also writes E3 = search_policy("monitors") and E4 = read_policy(E3.policy_ref), followed by the instruction to compare the evidence in E2 and E4.
Workers run the permitted searches and bind E1 and E3 to their results. Each read waits for its own policy reference, then supplies the corresponding text.
The solver receives the question, plan, and filled evidence variables. It returns a comparison grounded in the two passages.

The changing policy references are data in an already written plan. The planner did not inspect the first result to invent a new next action. This is the distinction from ReAct’s observation-driven loop. The ReWOO paper uses numbered evidence slots such as #E1; E1 through E4 are simplified labels for this trace.
If a search returns no allowed match, the corresponding read has no valid reference. In an application, a failure check must block that read and choose recovery or an evidence-gap response. A solver must not treat an unfilled variable as evidence. These are application requirements, not a guarantee supplied by the method.
ReWOO fits work whose tool sequence can be described in advance, even when later arguments depend on earlier results. Xu et al. identify a limit when the environment is too unknown to plan useful work ahead of observations.8 Tests should compare the checked result, missing or wrongly filled slots, planner calls, total tokens, and recovery cost with the observation-driven baseline.

10  Planning and coordinating agents

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
10.4 Plan-and-Act: revising plans from observations
The ReAct loop in Section 9.3 chooses again after each observation without requiring a separate remaining-work list. A stored plan makes unfinished work visible and lets planning and execution use different model calls. Its revision must still follow the objective and the latest permitted observations.
Erdogan et al. study Plan-and-Act for web navigation. A planner writes high-level steps; an executor turns them into concrete actions using the current page. Their dynamic replanning variant updates the remaining plan after each executor step, using current state and previous plans and actions. The paper also trains separate planner and executor models from generated and grounded examples. That training setup is part of the method, not supplied by adding a generic replanner function.9
For an illustrative policy lookup, the initial plan is to search and open the matching product policy. Search returns a monitor policy first and the headphone policy second. The planner now replaces the vague remaining step with an instruction to open the headphone result identified in the observation. The executor opens that result, and the application checks the product and source before accepting the answer. A changed instruction is useful only if the observation supports it.
The figure shows this separation of a plan, completed work, observations, and revision. It is a generic application design, not a reproduction of the paper’s trained system.






Figure 10.2: Replanning uses completed steps and observations to revise remaining work. This example returns a final answer when the objective is met and policy is satisfied.



The replan node is the defining addition. A static plan-and-execute system cannot absorb newly discovered constraints without a separate correction path.
The following generic replanner applies this distinction between remaining work and a final response. It does not implement the paper’s training or browser executor.
This abbreviated Python example assumes that state has the fields read below and that objective_satisfied, policy_satisfied, compose_answer, and revise_using are supplied by the application. It returns a Plan or Response. The application validates the incoming state before calling it. A final response needs both objective and policy checks. The revise_using helper must check that its proposed steps are executable and unfinished, using the objective, completed steps, and observations. The fragment checks only that its result is a nonempty list of nonblank strings. It raises ValueError on an empty or malformed result for the surrounding workflow to stop or escalate. It does not turn an empty plan into success.

Code example: A replanner returns either remaining work or a final response.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Plan:
    steps: list[str]

@dataclass
class Response:
    response: str

def replan(state) -> Plan | Response:
    if objective_satisfied(state) and policy_satisfied(state):
        return Response(response=compose_answer(state))
    remaining = revise_using(
        objective=state.objective,
        original_plan=state.original_plan,
        completed=state.past_steps,
        observations=state.observations,
    )
    if (not isinstance(remaining, list) or not remaining
            or any(not isinstance(step, str) or not step.strip()
                   for step in remaining)):
        raise ValueError("no valid unfinished steps")
    return Plan(steps=remaining)

Plan-state invariant
The plan should contain only unfinished work. Completed steps and their observations belong in execution history, and the final response should be produced only when the objective and policy checks pass.

Replanning can recover from a stale plan but adds model calls and can introduce new errors. Evaluation compares checked task outcomes, invalid revisions, calls, latency, and total cost with a fixed plan and with the ReAct baseline on the same tasks. A failed objective or policy check cannot become success merely because the revised list is empty.

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
10.5 LLMCompiler: dependency-aware scheduling
The replanner in Section 10.4 returns remaining steps or a final response. Running the steps one at a time makes independent tasks wait, which can increase wall-clock time. A dependency graph states which outputs each task needs, allowing a scheduler to run ready independent tasks concurrently and combine results after their prerequisites finish.

Task DAG: A directed acyclic graph whose nodes are executable tasks and whose edges state that one task depends on another task’s output.

Kim et al.10 report speed and cost improvements from LLMCompiler on the tasks and tool sets in their study. Its planner can stream tasks and dependencies, its scheduler replaces references to earlier outputs with their actual values, and its executor runs ready calls. A final combination step produces an answer or requests more planning. These results are not universal guarantees. Parallel calls shorten latency only when resources permit overlap, and they need not reduce the number of tool calls or their price.
Let \(G\) be the task graph, \(\pi\) one dependency-respecting path through it, and \(t_v\) the duration of task \(v\). Even with unlimited workers, the graph cannot complete sooner than its longest dependency path:
\[
T_{DAG}\ge\max_{\pi\in\mathrm{paths}(G)}\sum_{v\in\pi}t_v
\tag{10.1}\]
Here, \(T_{DAG}\) is the elapsed time to finish the graph and all durations use seconds. Each path follows task dependencies. This is a lower-bound latency model for the declared graph and task durations. Scheduling overhead, resource contention, and retries can add time. A final synthesis or join that takes time must be a node in the graph, as in the example below. Only work outside the graph adds a further join cost.

Example: Critical path versus serial execution
Three independent document summaries take 8, 6, and 5 seconds. A final synthesis depends on all three and takes 4 seconds. Assume at least three available workers, unchanged task durations, and no scheduling overhead or shared-resource conflict.

Serial execution takes 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 23 seconds before overhead.
In a dependency graph, the three summaries can start together.
The longest prerequisite path is max(8, 6, 5) + 4 = 12 seconds.

Result: The idealized graph reduces the dependency-limited time from 23 seconds to 12 seconds.
Interpretation: The gain exists because the summaries are independent. Mislabeling a real dependency can make the faster schedule produce an invalid result.
The timeline below depicts these same three summaries and their final synthesis, using the same durations and assumptions.







Figure 10.3: With enough workers and no scheduling overhead, parallel summaries reduce this example’s ideal time from 23 s to the 12 s critical path.



The scheduler needs a concrete rule for determining which unfinished nodes may run at scheduler time t.
\[
\mathrm{Ready}(t)=\{v:v\notin\mathrm{Done}(t),\mathrm{Pred}(v)\subseteq\mathrm{Done}(t)\}
\tag{10.2}\]
Here, \(\operatorname{Done}(t)\) denotes completed nodes, while \(\operatorname{Pred}(v)\) represents predecessor nodes. In the batch scheduler below, the expression is checked only after the previous batch has completed. It selects unfinished nodes whose predecessors are finished. An asynchronous dispatcher must also exclude nodes already running. Readiness proves dependency completion only. Authorization, rate limits, and safe concurrency require independent checks.

Example: Ready nodes after one dependency completes
A graph contains A -> B, A -> C, and both B and C -> D. Only A is complete.

B’s predecessor set is {A}, which is contained in Done(t).
C’s predecessor set is also {A}, which is contained in Done(t).
D requires both B and C, so D is not ready.

Result: The ready set contains B and C, allowing them to run concurrently.
Interpretation: The scheduler exposes parallelism already present in the dependency graph. It cannot safely invent independence that the plan did not establish.

The following loop turns dependency readiness into a dispatch rule.
This abbreviated Python loop assumes task objects with id and dependencies, an initially empty results mapping, and application-supplied run_in_parallel and joiner. The runner returns one successful result per dispatched task and raises on execution failure. The loop rejects duplicate task IDs, references to missing tasks, cycles, and incomplete batches. It returns the joiner’s answer only after all tasks succeed. Authorization, timeouts, cancellation, and resource-safe concurrency belong in the runner and are not implemented here.

Code example: A scheduler dispatches only tasks whose dependencies are satisfied.

class InvalidPlan(ValueError):
    pass

class TaskFailure(RuntimeError):
    pass

def ready_tasks(tasks, results):
    return [
        task for task in tasks
        if task.id not in results
        and all(dep in results for dep in task.dependencies)
    ]

task_ids = [task.id for task in tasks]
if len(task_ids) != len(set(task_ids)):
    raise InvalidPlan("duplicate task ID")
if any(dep not in task_ids
       for task in tasks for dep in task.dependencies):
    raise InvalidPlan("missing dependency ID")
if results:
    raise InvalidPlan("this example requires empty initial results")

while len(results) < len(tasks):
    batch = ready_tasks(tasks, results)
    if not batch:
        raise InvalidPlan("cycle in unfinished tasks")
    batch_results = run_in_parallel(batch, results)
    if (not isinstance(batch_results, dict)
            or set(batch_results) != {task.id for task in batch}):
        raise TaskFailure("batch did not return every dispatched result")
    results.update(batch_results)

answer = joiner(results)
The loop keeps invalid plan structure separate from an incomplete execution batch. It rejects missing IDs before dispatch and reports a cycle when unfinished tasks have no ready node. A full scheduler also records each task’s success, failure, or cancellation separately. A failed prerequisite must never count as a completed successful dependency. Its dependents are cancelled or blocked according to policy. These outcomes need different repairs and should remain distinct in the trace.

Graph evaluation
Graph evaluation tests dependency correctness, peak concurrency, critical-path latency, joiner faithfulness, cancellation, and partial failure. An end-answer score alone cannot reveal whether apparent speed came from skipping required work.

The graph must also declare which resources each task reads and writes, how cancellation is propagated, and what the join step requires. An undeclared state change can make two apparently independent nodes conflict. A sequential reference run provides a comparison until tests show that the parallel schedule preserves the required state and result.

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
10.6 Reflexion: feedback between attempts
A plan can execute as written and still produce the wrong answer. Repeating the attempt with no information about its failure can repeat the same mistake. Reflexion adds a feedback note that the agent receives on a later attempt. Shinn et al. separate the acting agent, an evaluator of the attempt, and a reflection step that turns the attempt and feedback into a verbal correction. Model weights stay unchanged.11
The process has three results to keep distinct: the attempted answer or action trace, the evaluator’s finding, and the generated reflection. The finding is evidence about the attempt. The reflection is a proposed lesson, which may itself be wrong. The next attempt uses that lesson along with the task and permitted evidence.
Suppose the policy-comparison agent returns a headphone deadline but cites the monitor policy. An illustrative sequence is:

A checker compares the product in the question with the cited passage and rejects the attempt.
The reflection step writes, “I selected a similar title without checking the product. On the next attempt, read the passage and verify the category before using its deadline.”
The application keeps that note with this task’s attempt history. The next attempt receives it and obtains the correct product’s passage.
The checker evaluates the new answer independently. The retry stops on a pass, the attempt limit, or another stop condition.

This trace illustrates feedback across attempts, not a measured improvement. A bad checker could produce an unhelpful lesson, and a new attempt can still fail. Evaluation therefore compares checked outcomes and total cost with retries that do not receive reflection notes. Raising the evaluator’s score alone is insufficient if the answer remains wrong.
The feedback patterns in Chapter 8 revise a candidate against criteria. Reflexion specifically carries a verbal lesson into a later attempt. It can wrap a ReAct-style agent rather than replace its action loop. A task’s saved note also need not become permanent user memory. Reusing it across sessions requires the storage, access, correction, and deletion rules in Chapter 11.

10  Planning and coordinating agents

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
10.7 When extra agents are warranted
A support application may need billing and account-access tools with different permissions and instructions. Placing them in separate agent loops can reduce the choices each model sees. Application code must still decide which loop runs, what it may read or change, and when the whole task is complete. The extra loops add routing calls, transferred state, and duplicated context, so evaluation must test route selection, state transfer, loop detection, and incomplete results after worker failure.

Multi-agent system: A controlled composition of two or more agent loops with explicit communication, state access, routing, and termination rules enforced by the surrounding application.

Four recurring limitations provide concrete reasons to consider that composition:

Tool overload: one agent prompt can contain so many similar tools that selection degrades.
Context bloat: unrelated domain instructions and evidence compete in one context window.
Serial bottleneck: independent subtasks dominate wall-clock time when executed by one loop.
Separate teams or permissions: different domains need different responsible teams, permissions, release schedules, or compliance rules.


Escalation test
A decision to add agents needs a task requirement or measured single-agent limit, a prediction of which multi-agent pattern addresses it, and tests for the new failure modes.







Figure 10.4: The patterns differ in who directs work and receives results. Solid arrows show task or control transfer, dashed arrows show returns, and gray routes show other permitted handoffs. Application checks govern permissions, budgets, and termination in every pattern.



In an orchestrator-worker pattern, a central router selects a worker and receives its result. A hierarchy adds routers for separate domains. In a network, agents have permitted peer links. Here, swarm means one worker selects the next worker without a central router. It does not mean that every worker runs at once. These categories can overlap: network describes the available links, while this use of swarm describes how control passes along them. The figure sketches connections and control choices, not four mutually exclusive topologies or complete runtime graphs. The table compares task dependencies, permissions, routing delay, and failure handling. These conditions guide an engineering choice; they do not guarantee the best pattern.
Anthropic12 reported that a research system using Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 workers outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2 percent on its internal research evaluation. Separately, it reported about 15 times as many tokens for multi-agent systems as for chat interactions. The different baselines matter: 15 times is not the reported token ratio for the evaluated single-agent comparison. The report also notes that shared-context tasks and tasks with many dependencies between agents can fit this approach poorly.



Table 10.2: Communication links and control policies can be combined; each needs explicit routing and termination checks.











Pattern
Who selects the next agent?
Conditions that can favor the pattern
Risks to test




Network
Routing policy selects; peer links alone do not choose
Small exploratory debate or research groups
A fully connected set of N agents allows N(N-1) directed peer links and many possible interactions


Orchestrator-worker
A central router
Central routing across specialized workers
Router latency, misrouting, and supervisor drift


Hierarchical
Routers at multiple domain levels
Large organizations or many isolated domains
Multiple routing layers, latency, and error propagation


Swarm
The active worker hands off directly
Stateful conversations with infrequent domain shifts
Ping-pong handoffs and hidden global completion state







Debate-style evaluation
The course’s evaluation lecture describes a debate-style way to judge candidate answers. One role argues for answer A, another for answer B, and a referee judges both against the scoring rules. This can be a fixed evaluation workflow, not separate tool-using agent loops. It illustrates a different reason to divide model work: comparing criticisms of the same answer rather than assigning independent product tasks.
Agreement does not establish correctness. The referee’s decisions still need comparison with trusted labels or expert review, calibration, and cases that expose shared mistakes. The debate adds calls and cost; its value is whether it improves checked judgments over a simpler evaluator, not whether it produces longer arguments.

10  Planning and coordinating agents

title: 10  Planning and coordinating agents
text:
10.8 Agent handoffs and return control
A pattern describes the possible communication paths. A concrete system still needs a mechanism for changing the active agent loop without losing user intent, authorization, or progress. A handoff identifies the destination, transfers only the required state, records the output expected from that loop, and states where control returns.
Application code checks the destination, task, completion criteria, return route, and authorization before changing the active loop. It loads only evidence the destination may read and records the accepted handoff with the resulting state. The typed record below is an application design, not an MCP message type. MCP standardizes tool and context exchanges (Section 9.7), not this record’s task and return-control rules.
This abbreviated Python 3.10-or-later example needs application-supplied helpers and a state object.
The supplied helpers have these required behaviors. validate_destination rejects unknown workers. validate_authorization checks that the authority covers this task and destination. load_refs checks access to each reference and enforces the application’s payload-size limit. transfer_control must save the accepted record and changed state together, or fail without applying either.
An empty evidence list is allowed for a task that needs no external evidence. Literal documents labels but does not validate them at runtime. The explicit checks reject empty task fields, invalid return labels, and malformed reference lists.
Helper failures before transfer_control leave the active agent unchanged. The fragment does not run a worker or grant permission for its later tool actions, which need the checks from Section 8.7.

Code example: The checked handoff retains the task and return route with evidence loaded under application access and size limits.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

@dataclass
class Handoff:
    destination: Literal["billing", "auth", "notifier"]
    reason: str
    task: str
    completion_criteria: str
    evidence_refs: list[str]
    authorization_ref: str | None
    return_to: Literal["orchestrator", "user", "none"]

def accept_handoff(handoff: Handoff, state):
    validate_destination(handoff.destination)
    for value in (handoff.reason, handoff.task, handoff.completion_criteria):
        if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("handoff fields must be nonempty strings")
    if handoff.return_to not in {"orchestrator", "user", "none"}:
        raise ValueError("invalid return route")
    if not isinstance(handoff.evidence_refs, list) or any(
        not isinstance(ref, str) or not ref.strip()
        for ref in handoff.evidence_refs
    ):
        raise ValueError("invalid evidence references")
    validate_authorization(
        handoff.authorization_ref, handoff.task,
        destination=handoff.destination,
    )
    context = load_refs(
        handoff.evidence_refs, destination=handoff.destination,
        authorization_ref=handoff.authorization_ref,
    )
    return state.transfer_control(
        active_agent=handoff.destination,
        bounded_context=context,
        task=handoff.task,
        reason=handoff.reason,
        completion_criteria=handoff.completion_criteria,
        authorization_ref=handoff.authorization_ref,
        evidence_refs=list(handoff.evidence_refs),
        return_to=handoff.return_to,
    )
For an illustrative handoff, an orchestrator sends billing the task “check this order’s refund eligibility”, its policy reference, and the completion criterion to return eligibility with the policy source. The accepted state retains that task, authority reference, evidence references, and the route back to the orchestrator. A rejected authority reference stops execution before evidence is loaded or control changes. After the worker returns, the orchestrator checks the criterion before marking the task complete. The table lists further failure controls, such as handoff budgets and worker-status checks, that this fragment does not implement.



Table 10.3: Handoff failures are state and control failures.










Failure
Observable symptom
Mitigation




Routing oscillation
Agents hand control back and forth without new evidence
Handoff budget, visited-route state, and loop detection


Context loss
Destination repeats work or misreads user intent
Typed task, evidence references, constraints, and completion criteria


Supervisor drift
Central router begins solving domain work itself
Narrow router outputs and separate route-accuracy evaluation

One worker fails but synthesis sounds complete

Reduce permissions to the task and destination, then recheck each proposed action






A whole-run trace connects delegated tasks, not just accepted transfers. Each task has an identifier, a parent task, completion criteria, and a status. Tool-call records link to that task and retain permitted argument details, result status, duration, and failure or stop reason. The return record links the worker’s result to the caller’s completion check. This lets an evaluator follow a wrong final answer back through delegation and tool execution, or identify work left unfinished after a worker fails. Chapter 13 develops logging and trace records; the handoff record alone is not that complete trace.
A bounded handoff carries only the state needed by the next agent loop. It ends with a checked return or a recorded failure, not merely a message sent to a worker. Reusing selected information in later sessions creates the separate storage problem in Chapter 11.

Chapter conclusion
Planning organizes proposed work; execution checks whether each permitted step succeeded. Coordination determines which agent loop receives a task and what counts as a valid return. More planning or more agents are useful only when their checked results justify the added calls, context, and failure paths. Chapter 11 examines a different decision: which information from these runs may be reused in later sessions.

title: 11  Persistent memory across sessions
text:
11.1 Memory storage and reuse
A later conversation may need information from an earlier one: a delivery preference, the outcome of a support request, or a procedure tested in a previous release. That information should not be copied into every request or kept forever by default. Persistent memory is information stored for reuse across sessions. The application decides which information may be stored, who may retrieve it, and how it is corrected or removed.
The map follows storage and reuse, dated events, current facts, correction and deletion, and versioned procedures. Chapter 9’s session checkpoint restores an unfinished run. This chapter asks what may be reused beyond that session. A checkpoint can be durable without becoming a user profile or permission to reuse its contents for another task.
A later session may need a preference, an earlier event, or a tested procedure that is absent from the current request. The application needs rules for choosing what may be stored and reused. Without those rules, it may save every message and later supply stale, irrelevant, or unauthorized information.
RAG in Chapter 6 supplies a read path: find permitted evidence and place it in a request. A memory system may use that same retrieval machinery. It also needs a write path: capture a candidate, check whether it may become durable, and later correct, expire, or delete it. Similarity search alone does not make those decisions.
Sumers et al.1 distinguish four memory roles: active task state, records of earlier events, facts, and knowledge of how to act. Their framework includes both current state and longer-term knowledge. The following descriptions apply those roles to this application’s choices about storing, reviewing, and versioning information. Saving task state for recovery does not automatically permit reuse in another session. These roles do not require four physical databases.
Persistent records can retain information that cannot be reconstructed from the current request, such as a previously stated preference. Reuse is worthwhile when the information is relevant, permitted, and current enough for the task, and its benefit justifies storage, retrieval, and review costs.
These categories help the application apply different storage and reuse rules. Separation alone enforces no rule: capture and promotion checks determine whether a past message may become a durable, reusable fact.

title: 11  Persistent memory across sessions
text:
Working memory: The active state for the current task, including goals, plans, evidence, tool definitions, and observations. The application selects part of it for each model request.
Episodic memory: Timestamped records of earlier interactions, actions, and outcomes that an application may retrieve for a later request.
Semantic memory: Curated facts or preferences that an application stores separately from the events from which they were derived.
Procedural memory: The agent’s model parameters and reusable code or instructions that determine how it performs a task.





Table 11.1: Memory roles, example stores, and application control questions.











Memory type
Content
Typical store
Key control question




Working
Active task state, messages, plan, and tool observations
Application state with a selected portion in the request context
What deserves scarce context tokens now?


Episodic
Timestamped interactions and outcomes
Event log or vector/time index
Which past event is relevant and permitted?


Semantic
Curated facts and preferences
Profile, knowledge graph, or fact store
Is the fact valid, scoped, current, and correctable?


Procedural

Model parameters and versioned code or instruction assets

Memory system: The database, index, and application logic that manages persistent state across agent sessions.
Capture: The process of identifying candidate information from the conversation and associating it with a source.
Promotion: The policy-controlled decision to store a captured candidate as a durable fact or procedure after checking its source, identity, scope, confidence, retention rule, and required human approval.

title: 11  Persistent memory across sessions
text:
11.2 Episodic memory: retrieving earlier events
A later question may need one event from a long conversation rather than the whole history. Working memory holds active task state, while episodic memory keeps dated events that the application may retrieve into that state. The request context contains only the selected portion that fits alongside instructions and reserved output space.
Irrelevant history can crowd out policy, evidence, and output space even when it fits within the context window.
The application selects system policy, current objectives, active plans, retrieved evidence, tool definitions, and relevant observations for the next request. It reserves output tokens separately. Summaries can reduce history size, but may lose details, so important claims should retain references to their source events. To preserve a commitment across turns, the application can store a separate record of the promise, responsible party, approval condition, and source event. It can retrieve that record when relevant, under rules for correction, review, access, and deletion.
Semantic similarity alone is weak for temporal questions. Episodic retrieval often needs user, session, time, entity, and access filters alongside embeddings.
An episodic store captures event identity, timestamps, actor roles, actions, observations, and the source record. Retrieval applies user and access filters before ranking, and time or entity filters when the question requires them. For example, “which delivery address did I give before the move?” needs the correct user’s events from before the move, not merely the most similar address message. The application loads the selected event into working memory and preserves its date in the answer evidence. A summary should retain a stable source reference while the source may be kept. If that source expires or is deleted, the summary must be removed, updated, or excluded according to the same policy.
Conversation history is user data, not free application context. The accountable product owner or data policy owner defines retention and deletion rules, and application code enforces them when storing, retrieving, expiring, and deleting records. Evaluation should measure episodic recall, irrelevant records injected into context, harm from stale facts, and compliance with the applicable rules.

title: 11  Persistent memory across sessions
section: 11.3 Semantic memory: promoting and ranking facts
text:
11.3 Semantic memory: promoting and ranking facts
Episodic memory preserves dated events and their outcomes. Raw events do not automatically become reliable current facts, especially when observations conflict or user preferences change. Semantic memory introduces an explicit promotion and correction process before a fact becomes reusable across sessions.
Storing extracted statements without review can create duplicate, stale, conflicting, and mis-scoped profile records. Promotion therefore needs a schema, confidence rule, scope, source record, conflict policy, and correction path.






Figure 11.2: Promotion policy permits direct storage, requires human review, or rejects the candidate. Rejection creates no semantic record; the original episode remains only while its retention and deletion rules permit.



The promotion step is an application policy. The model may propose a candidate memory, but deterministic code or human review decides whether it becomes durable.
After identity, permission, status, and deletion filters remove ineligible records, the application ranks remaining records by relevance, freshness, and source reliability.
\[
S(m,q)=w_r\mathrm{relevance}(m,q)+w_f\mathrm{freshness}(m)+w_s\mathrm{reliability}(m)
\tag{11.1}\]
Here, \(m\) is an eligible record and \(q\) is the request. The component functions return relevance, freshness, and reliability scores. Product weights \(w_r\), \(w_f\), and \(w_s\) balance these scores to rank candidates without overriding access rules.
Freshness needs a defined clock and a valid observation time. This example rejects future observed_at values and computes a nonnegative age in days when the record is read. With a 30-day useful-life horizon, freshness is the larger of zero and 1 - age_in_days / 30. A record observed 6 days ago receives 0.8, while one at least 30 days old receives 0 and should normally be refreshed or excluded. An expires_at rule can remove a record before ranking. The 30-day horizon is only an example. It must reflect how quickly the underlying fact changes. The application compares the ranking with reviewed retrieval choices. The score is not a probability of truth.
In the example below, each component uses a 0 to 1 scale, and the weights express the product’s chosen trade-off. Another design can use other scales or weights that do not sum to one.

Example: Rank two eligible memory records
Suppose two permitted records can help answer a question. The weights are 0.5 for relevance, 0.3 for freshness, and 0.2 for source reliability. Record A scores 0.8, 0.6, and 1.0; Record B scores 0.9, 0.2, and 0.8. Under the 30-day freshness rule, A’s score of 0.6 represents a record 12 days old.

Record A: 0.5 × 0.8 + 0.3 × 0.6 + 0.2 × 1.0 = 0.78.
Record B: 0.5 × 0.9 + 0.3 × 0.2 + 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.67.

Result: Record A ranks above B despite B’s higher relevance.
Interpretation: The chosen weights trade some relevance for freshness and source reliability. The arithmetic does not establish that this trade-off improves answers, which needs reviewed retrieval tests. A deleted, unauthorized, or wrong-subject record remains ineligible regardless of its score.

This Python record describes a fact’s fields, not a validator. For a stored delivery address, subject_id identifies the user. The predicate is delivery_address, and value contains the address. The application defines identity, category, intended-use scope, source tracking, and retention rules. source_episode_ids identifies the conversations or events from which the fact was derived. The provenance field holds references to supporting records checked during validation. The dataclass constructor requires the declared fields, but does not check their annotated types or allowed values. The store must validate the status, identity, scope, confidence, and dates before accepting the record.

Code example: A semantic fact record carries lifecycle metadata.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Literal

@dataclass
class MemoryFact:
    subject_id: str
    predicate: str
    value: str
    category: str
    scope: str
    source_episode_ids: list[str]
    provenance: list[str]
    confidence: float
    observed_at: datetime
    created_at: datetime
    reviewed_at: datetime | None
    expires_at: datetime | None
    status: Literal["candidate", "active", "superseded", "deleted"]

title: 11  Persistent memory across sessions
text:
11.4 Correction and deletion
The record describes what a fact stores. The next fragment shows when the application may store it and how deletion reaches the locations that serve it.

Tombstone: A small record stating that an item was deleted or replaced, without retaining the removed value. Replicas and indexes use it to avoid restoring an old copy during synchronization.

This abbreviated Python fragment uses MemoryFact and application-supplied policy, validation, store, index, cache, and audit helpers. require raises on a failed condition. validate_candidate checks the record’s values and supporting evidence. The caller then checks that validation has not changed its subject, category, or scope, and stores the whole validated record as active with the policy’s expiry. This example requires category consent, although another product may use a different approved authority. authorize_delete checks the caller and record before removal. Helper exceptions propagate to the surrounding workflow, which must record partial cleanup and retry it. The fragment has no automatic retry or cross-store transaction.

Code example: Promotion stores the complete active fact. Deletion cleans the listed stores in sequence and reports completion only after those calls succeed.

from dataclasses import replace

def promote_memory(candidate: MemoryFact, user):
    require(candidate.status == "candidate")
    require(candidate.subject_id == user.id)
    require(candidate.source_episode_ids and candidate.provenance)
    require(isinstance(candidate.observed_at, datetime))
    require(user.consent_for(candidate.category))
    approved_use = (candidate.subject_id, candidate.category, candidate.scope)
    verified = validate_candidate(candidate)
    require(verified.status == "candidate")
    require((verified.subject_id, verified.category, verified.scope) == approved_use)
    active = replace(
        verified, status="active", expires_at=retention_policy(verified),
    )
    return memory_store.put(active)

def delete_memory(user, memory_id):
    authorize_delete(user, memory_id)
    memory_store.tombstone(user.id, memory_id)
    derived_indexes.remove(memory_id)
    cache.invalidate(memory_id)
    deletion_audit.record_without_value(user.id, memory_id)
    return {"status": "deleted", "memory_id": memory_id}
Promotion retains the fact’s identity, predicate, value, supporting records, confidence, dates, and intended-use scope. Deletion follows three stages:

Mark the primary record deleted.
Remove its index entries and cache copy.
After every listed cleanup step succeeds, return deleted and write the value-free completion audit.

If index removal fails, the exception stops later calls, so the cache may still contain the value and no completed-deletion audit is written. Reads must check the primary deletion status even during cleanup. The helpers must make repeated cleanup safe, as Section 8.2 explains for idempotent operations. Replicas, backups, exports, and other copies need separate removal or restoration rules. The audit records completion of the listed steps, not proof that every copy everywhere was erased.

Correction rule
When a new fact conflicts with an active fact, check identity, intended use, observation time, and supporting records. If the new value is a correction, mark the old record superseded and make it ineligible for retrieval. Otherwise, retain it only for a distinct valid use. Keep the change visible to the user when appropriate.

A candidate statement may remain in the episodic record while its retention rules permit. Evidence, consent where relevant, confidence, and intended use determine whether it can be promoted to a durable profile fact. Failure to promote it does not authorize keeping it indefinitely.
Conflict resolution compares identity, time, source reliability, and whether the new statement corrects or supplements the old one. For example, a user’s new delivery address supersedes the old address for current deliveries, while the old event may still support a permitted question about a past order. Superseded facts are excluded from current-fact retrieval and stay traceable only while retention permits. Wu et al.2 use LongMemEval to test temporal updates, multi-session reasoning, and abstention when the needed information is absent. Product evaluation also measures retrieval utility, stale-fact use, correction success, cross-user isolation, and deletion propagation.

section: 11.5 Procedural memory: versioned instructions and tools
text:
11.5 Procedural memory: versioned instructions and tools
Correcting a stored fact changes what the application knows about a user or event. Changing a reusable instruction or tool can alter every later action that uses it. The application retrieves semantic records as task context, while versioned prompts, tools, and workflows determine which actions the agent loop can propose. These procedures need tests and release controls before a new version runs.
A reusable workflow encoded as a tool or instruction asset saves the agent from re-deriving behavior. It can also preserve a mistake indefinitely. The application therefore records the procedure version with every run and uses conformance tests. A user preference belongs in semantic memory, while a system rule belongs in procedural memory.
Suppose procedure version 1 creates a refund draft and version 2 adds a new eligibility check. Review compares the rule with the approved policy, tests permitted and denied cases, and releases version 2 only if those checks pass. Each execution records version 2 and its result. If monitoring reveals a regression, the application stops affected work and restores a tested version that still satisfies current policy. Rolling back to an obsolete policy would not be a valid recovery. This is an illustrative release trace, not a measured improvement.
The table brings together the chapter’s memory controls, from capture to expiration or deletion.



Table 11.2: Memory quality requires capture-to-forgetting controls.










Lifecycle stage
Memory question
Evidence




Capture
What event or candidate fact is worth storing?
Eligibility rule, required authority, supporting source, sensitivity label


Promote
Should this candidate become a durable fact or procedure?
Validation, confidence, review where required, and intended-use scope


Retrieve
Which memory is relevant to this task and user?
Filters, rank, freshness, authorization, token cost


Use
How did memory affect the decision or answer?
Injected memory IDs and trace attribution


Correct
How are conflicts, user corrections, and stale data handled?
Supersession record and regression test


Forget
When must data expire or be deleted?
Retention schedule, cleanup status, downstream removal, and restore rules







Chapter conclusion
Persistent memory selects information for later sessions under rules for storage, access, correction, and deletion. RAG can retrieve those records, but retrieval does not decide which records may exist or remain current. Procedures need reviewed versions and tests because a saved instruction can change future actions, not just future answers.

title: Part V - System cases, diagnosis, and release decisions
text:
Chapters in this part
A release decision concerns the complete system, not one prompt, retriever, model, or tool in isolation. The evidence must show which component produced each result, which failures remain, and how the system behaves within its time, cost, and safety limits.
This Part combines task definitions, evaluation results, retrieval traces, tool steps, saved-state changes, cost and latency into system cases. The execution logs support investigating failures, choosing a sufficient design and deciding whether release requirements are met.
Chapter 12 follows evaluation, RAG, and support-agent cases through their logs and checks, then tests a small runnable subset with local stand-ins. Chapter 13 explains stage-specific logging, established standards and logging tools. Chapter 14 connects architecture choices and failure diagnosis to release requirements for quality, evidence support, tool control, infrastructure, cost and latency.

12.1 Example systems and their architecture
A plausible final answer can hide a failed evaluator, missed evidence, unauthorized access, or an incorrect tool call. The three examples combine evaluation, retrieved evidence, and controlled tool use. Their records show which steps need checking when the final result is wrong.
The map compares a product-description evaluator, a RAG pipeline that cites selected evidence, and a controlled support-data agent through their evaluation and execution records.
A release reviewer needs different evidence for a generated description, a document answer, and a dataset count. These examples combine the components established earlier:
A generated description can fail at the prompt, model, or evaluator. A grounded answer adds ingestion, indexing, retrieval, context assembly, and citation. A data agent adds routing, tool execution, state transitions, budgets, and persistence. The evidence record grows with the system because each additional component supplies another possible cause for the same visible failure.
The figure separates document preparation, retrieval, model access, output checks, and tools. Appendix A describes the libraries at those positions. Application code must check the caller’s permissions before retrieving private records or executing a tool. In this illustrated deployment, the model runs as a separate service. Section 1.5 compares a provider API, a managed platform, and self-hosting. API compatibility, supported parameters, and service controls must be checked for the chosen endpoint rather than assumed identical across those options.
The product-description evaluator uses only the model path and the evaluation band. The RAG pipeline adds ingestion and retrieval. The support-data agent adds orchestration, tools, and checked tool calls.

title: 12  Integrated AI system cases
text:
12.2 Product evaluation and verifiable evidence
A generated product description has no single reference string that captures quality. Section 5.7 established the evaluation pipeline for this task, including rubric definitions, versioned run records, judge-model calibration, and rater-agreement metrics. The integrated pipeline retains that evidence for a release decision alongside cost, latency, and policy checks.
The release harness reuses the rubric anchors and pass rules established during evaluation design. Each generated output links to its prompt version, model identifier, execution latency, and token counts. Programmatic checks score schema validity and budget compliance. A model judge scores subjective criteria only where it meets the evaluation protocol’s agreement rule on a held-out human-labeled subset. Agreement alone does not establish correctness, as Section 5.4 explains.
The evidence record includes explanatory notes, executable prompts and model setup, data-processing functions, and row-level manual and automated scores. It also retains failed experiments and their conditions so later reviewers can treat a negative result as evidence and avoid repeating the same change without a new hypothesis.
The table describes the judge’s output format and the choice between separate and combined criterion calls.



Table 12.2: The evaluation example keeps subjective judgments separate from measured cost and latency.









Evaluation choice
Reason




Explanation first
The judge output places a criterion-specific explanation before the label so reviewers can check both.


Verdict second
The output schema limits the label to allowed values. Field order is a prompt convention, not proof that the explanation is correct.


Programmatic cost and latency outside the judge
Measured quantities should not be delegated to a subjective model.


Criterion-isolated judge runs
Comparing separate criterion calls with bundled calls tests whether the arrangement changes labels and human agreement.






The example produces two distinct outputs: a product description and an evaluation record. The description is user-visible, while the evaluation record contains the rubric version, generation settings, criterion labels, cost, latency, judge explanation, and agreement evidence. Keeping them separate allows the product output to remain concise without losing the information required for diagnosis.
Suppose the supplied product facts specify six hours of battery life, but the generated description claims twelve. The factual-accuracy criterion fails even if the output has valid fields and meets the cost limit. A criterion-level record preserves the unsupported claim and the supplied fact, rather than treating the other passing checks as evidence that the description is accurate.

title: 12  Integrated AI system cases
text:
12.3 RAG and support-agent traces
The evaluation example scored output generated from structured product facts. FinanceBench instead asks questions about public-company documents whose relevant facts may be absent, stale, or reproduced unreliably from the model’s learned parameters.1 A traced RAG pipeline records each stage of the evidence path so reviewers can attribute a poor answer to retrieval, context assembly, generation, or validation.

A no-retrieval run on a fixed question slice establishes correct, partially correct, wrong, and refusal outcomes for the baseline.
Dataset filtering limits ingestion to the referenced public documents. An explicit mapping gives each selected PDF its FinanceBench document ID before the loader attaches doc_name, company, period, and one-based source_page. The local page is the zero-based parser page plus one. The raw FinanceBench evidence page is also zero based and is converted before scoring.2 Each saved chunk gets an ID linked to its index build.
The baseline index records its embedding model, chunk size, overlap, and persistent FAISS storage configuration.
answer_with_rag is the online RAG function first developed in Section 6.7. It returns the ordered pre-reranking candidates and their FAISS distances, selected chunks, answer, and exact rendered request together. Empty retrieval or selection returns status: insufficient_evidence, with answer and rendered-request fields set to None and an empty selected list. If reranking selects nothing, the original candidates remain in the record.
The same questions pass through no-retrieval and RAG paths so retrieval changes without changing the evaluation set.
Final correctness, grounding faithfulness, and evidence-page hit remain separate per-question measurements before aggregation.
One-variable experiments vary prompt, model, k, chunk size, or reranking while retaining the same comparison slice.

This listing repeats the current Section 6.7 function unchanged. The application supplies the vector index, BGE reranker, prompt renderer, and generation model. The renderer must preserve the selected passages, and the generation adapter returns .text and .cited_pages. The function accepts integer k values from 1 to 12. This public-data example does not implement per-user retrieval permissions. Private records require access filtering before they enter the model request.

Code example: The integrated case reuses the Chapter 6 RAG interface and preserves retrieval evidence.

def answer_with_rag(question, *, k=5):
    if type(k) is not int or not 1 <= k <= 12:
        raise ValueError("k must be an integer from 1 to 12")
    retrieved = index.similarity_search_with_score(question, k=12)
    candidates = [
        {
            "index_build_id": doc.metadata["index_build_id"],
            "chunk_id": doc.metadata["chunk_id"],
            "citation_id": f"{doc.metadata['doc_name']}#p{doc.metadata['source_page']}",
            "faiss_distance": float(distance),
        }
        for doc, distance in retrieved
    ]
    if not retrieved:
        return {
            "question": question, "answer": None, "cited_pages": [],
            "candidates": [], "retrieved": [],
            "model_request": None, "k": k,
            "status": "insufficient_evidence",
        }
    reranked = bge_reranker.rerank(
        question,
        [doc for doc, _ in retrieved],
    )[:k]
    context = [
        {
            "chunk_text": doc.page_content,
            "index_build_id": doc.metadata["index_build_id"],
            "chunk_id": doc.metadata["chunk_id"],
            "doc_name": doc.metadata["doc_name"],
            "source_page": doc.metadata["source_page"],
            "citation_id": f"{doc.metadata['doc_name']}#p{doc.metadata['source_page']}",
            "reranker_score": score,
        }
        for doc, score in reranked
    ]
    if not context:
        return {
            "question": question, "answer": None, "cited_pages": [],
            "candidates": candidates, "retrieved": [],
            "model_request": None, "k": k,
            "status": "insufficient_evidence",
        }
    model_request = render_grounded_prompt(question=question, evidence=context)
    answer = generation_model(model_request)
    allowed_citations = {item["citation_id"] for item in context}
    cited_pages = list(answer.cited_pages)
    if not set(cited_pages) <= allowed_citations:
        raise ValueError("Answer cited evidence outside the supplied context")
    return {
        "question": question,
        "answer": answer.text,
        "cited_pages": cited_pages,
        "candidates": candidates,
        "retrieved": context,
        "model_request": model_request,
        "k": k,
        "status": "answered",
    }

Why the returned chunks matter
The candidate record preserves what search found before reranking. Selected records and the rendered request show what the application submitted to the model. Citation membership alone does not show that a cited passage supports the answer.

The retrieval trace connects status, question, candidates, answer, cited_pages, retrieved, model_request, and k. Candidate entries preserve index_build_id, chunk_id, citation_id, and faiss_distance in search-result order. Each selected entry adds chunk_text, doc_name, one-based source_page, and reranker_score. The build and chunk IDs resolve a candidate to its stored text even when two chunks share one page. Page-level citation IDs remain separate. A missed labeled page requires comparing source, parsing, chunking, indexing, ranking, and final-selection records to locate the omission. If selection contains the needed evidence, the rendered request distinguishes context assembly from generation and claim-support failures. Unknown citations raise ValueError, while helper failures propagate to the calling runner. Failed trials belong in the evaluation record.

12.4 Controlled tool choice
The RAG example used one evidence pipeline with a fixed request path. The support-data application must instead route each request among structured data tools, unstructured summarization, profile or history operations, and an out-of-scope decline. A dedicated router and small typed tool set keep that choice inside a graph whose decisions can be inspected.
Application checks govern the transitions between these components. The router receives the caller’s permitted task scope, tools check access and return typed observations, and downstream prompts receive checked results. A valid structure still needs permission and claim-support checks before it can justify an action or answer.
The table includes optional extensions. Restart tests apply when the design requires durable recovery; profile and MCP tests apply only when those features are enabled.

Layer
Application-enforced specification
Example acceptance test




Input and identity
Question, user ID, session ID, dataset scope
A restarted session restores only the matching conversation


Router
Structured, unstructured, profile, or out-of-scope labels for this example
Sports and CRM questions decline without data-tool calls


Tools
Names, descriptions, typed inputs, bounded results
get_refund filter followed by row count gives the expected total

Session state

Semantic profile

A corrected preference supersedes the old fact


MCP boundary

Evaluation

The support-data agent adds a policy-controlled choice about which capability to invoke next. Retrieval and dataset tools return evidence with identifiers. A final-state validator compares the answer with those results, while the trajectory records routes, calls, observations, budgets, and the stop reason. A direct count tool can answer a known count request without an agent loop. The two-tool case below shows one call passing a complete result reference to the next, at the cost of an extra call and temporary result storage.

title: 12  Integrated AI system cases
text:
12.6 Product evaluation across layers
A correct count can still follow unauthorized access. End-to-end cases include ordinary questions, adversarial access tests, ambiguous follow-ups, empty results, and tool errors. They also include restart scenarios when durable recovery is required and memory corrections when a profile is enabled. Reports lead with the validated final state, followed by the diagnostic trajectory and operational measures.



Table 12.4: End-to-end evaluation and component evaluation answer different questions.










Dimension
Representative metric
Failure question




Task outcome
Exact count, supported summary, correct decline, or completed state
Did the product achieve the user-visible objective?


Routing
Per-class precision, recall, and confusion matrix
Did the request enter the right policy and tool path?


Tool use
Tool-name accuracy, argument validity, result handling
Was the right capability used correctly?


Grounding
Claim support and evidence attribution
Does each factual claim follow from authorized observations?


Reliability
Success rate and interval across repeated trials
Is the behavior reproducible rather than a lucky trace?


Operations
p50/p95 latency, timeouts, token and tool cost
Can the product meet its service and budget target?


Safety and privacy
Unauthorized-call rate, approval compliance, deletion tests
Did the system enforce permissions and follow retention, correction, and deletion rules?






Outcome, component, and operational evaluation serve different decisions. Outcome metrics determine whether the request was completed safely and correctly. Component metrics identify which router, retriever, tool, validator, or memory layer contributed to a failure. Operational metrics determine whether the same behavior is reliable and affordable at the required latency.
A release decision links these three kinds of evaluation per case and per slice. Aggregate task success is accompanied by route confusion, tool-argument validity, evidence support, retry and fallback rates, p50 and p95 latency, cost, and policy events. Reviewers inspect those linked records for routing failures, excessive retries, and unauthorized actions even when the answer score is high.

title: 13  Logging system execution
text:
13.1 What to log at each stage
An answer or final tool result does not show how the application produced it. Logs preserve the inputs, decisions, outputs and failures needed to investigate that execution. Chapter 12’s cases show the request paths whose stages need logs.
A useful log lets a reviewer connect an outcome to the operations that produced it. Each request needs a shared identifier, with its steps and attempts identified separately. Nested or parallel work also needs parent or dependency links because timestamps alone do not show those relationships. Application code records event time, operation, component version, outcome and failure reason where applicable. Elapsed time belongs beside the operation it measures. These stage-specific fields apply established logging practices to the book’s examples. They are application choices. Some need logging code beyond the short examples.
These rows describe operations, rather than one mandatory sequence. Memory can be read before request assembly, and an agent can repeat retrieval and tool calls. The application logs only stages it uses and keeps each attempt distinct, including rejected, failed and timed-out attempts. A log containing only successful returns cannot explain the failed requests omitted from it.

title: 13  Logging system execution
text:
13.2 Established standards and practices
An event log describes an occurrence, such as a rejected tool argument. A trace links the operations belonging to a request, including nested or repeated steps. An evaluation log adds the test case, expected result, rubric and scores. Together they connect runtime behavior to the comparisons developed in Chapters 4, 5 and 7.
Services need shared ways to identify related work. Applications also need rules for what to log and how to protect it. These standards and practices address those needs:

W3C Trace Context standardizes the HTTP headers traceparent and tracestate used to pass trace context between services. This lets participating services associate their work with the same trace.1
OpenTelemetry defines a stable data model for logs, with timestamps, log levels, event details, extra fields and optional trace-context fields.2 A span describes one operation, with its start and end times and associated information. Spans link through parent and trace identifiers to show related work.3
OWASP’s Logging Cheat Sheet gives application logging guidance: capture enough information about when an event occurred, where it occurred, who initiated it and what happened. It includes validation, authorization and execution failures, and guidance on protecting the logs.4

These sources establish shared formats and logging practices. The table in Section 13.1 adds the domain information needed here, such as chunk IDs, candidate ranks and validation outcomes. Those fields must have documented meanings in the application. A shared trace identifier alone does not explain which passages entered a model request or whether a tool action was permitted.

13.3 Logging tools
Application code must log the stage information needed for diagnosis. A library cannot infer application details it has not received. A configured library integration may log model calls automatically. Application checks and state changes need additional logging code. The examples below cover event logging, tracing within and across services, and tracking evaluation runs with their settings and scores.

Tool
What it provides
What the application still supplies




logging with a configured formatter
Python event logging to outputs such as the console or files. Extra fields can accompany log entries.
The event schema, request/step IDs, permitted payloads and output format. JSON output needs serialization or a JSON formatter.


OpenTelemetry5
APIs and libraries for collecting logs and linked spans, plus software that sends them to a service for storage and analysis.
Application-specific fields, passing trace context between services, settings for sending the logs and spans, and a service for storage and analysis.

LLM-focused traces with linked observations for generation, retrieval and tools.

Experiment/run tracking with parameters, metrics and saved files (artifacts).
Evaluation definitions and results, run metadata, and the permitted log files to attach.






For a small script, structured local logs can be sufficient. Section 12.7 writes one JSON object per request on a separate line in traces.jsonl. Each object contains session_id, question, latency_ms and the current request’s trace. A session can contain several requests, so a separate request identifier is needed to link each one’s logs. The example preserves the request steps, but a complete logging setup also needs its version information and a way to retain partial logs when a helper fails.
For work across services, application code passes trace context and records spans to connect model, retrieval and tool operations. A tracing service can then display the timing and relationships between operations. For repeated evaluation runs, application code keeps parameters and scores linked to the permitted log files used to calculate them. The same request identifier can appear in the application log, its trace and its evaluation result.
These optional tools serve different logging needs. Their interfaces and integrations depend on the version. The earlier examples do not depend on these tools.

title: 13  Logging system execution
section: 13.4 Using logs to investigate a failure
text:
13.4 Using logs to investigate a failure
For the RAG example in Section 6.7, follow the candidate IDs into the selected passages and then into model_request. If a supporting passage was retrieved but omitted from that request, inspect selection and request assembly. If it entered the request but the answer contradicts it, inspect generation and answer validation. Section 7.1 develops these distinctions. A final answer and a search-success message alone cannot separate them.
For the workflow in Section 8.3, inspect the inputs, validation decisions and transition at each step. For a tool call, distinguish a proposed action from an attempted action and its actual result. For an agent, preserve the ordered attempts and stop reason. A failure in a helper needs a partial log even when the main function cannot return its normal result.
Decide which data may be stored in the logs, who may read the logs and how long they remain available. Exclude credentials and other prohibited data. Where full text cannot be logged, preserve permitted identifiers, versions and protected references. A hash can check whether data matches, but cannot recover its contents. OWASP also recommends testing logging failures and restricting access to the logs.8
Logs support investigation; they do not themselves establish that an answer is correct or an action is authorized. Chapter 14 uses the logged execution and its evaluation results as evidence for release decisions.

title: 14  Evidence for release decisions
text:
14.1 Smallest sufficient architecture
A candidate can give the right answer in a test and still use unauthorized data, repeat a tool call, or miss its latency target. A release review checks the complete result and the records of how the system produced it. The decision applies to one system version, its permitted inputs and actions, and the conditions tested.
The map connects architecture choices, failure diagnosis, a release record, and monitoring after release. Each stage uses evidence from the model, retrieval, tools, and memory only where the selected system needs them.
The examples in Chapter 12 combine different components for different tasks. Adding all of them to a new product would add costs and failure paths without necessarily improving the result. The choices below start from the task and its tests, then add capabilities for requirements the current design cannot meet. Products may need different combinations and execution orders.
For example, a fixed workflow can query a database and validate the result without document retrieval or an agent. Adding MCP changes how an allowed tool is discovered and called, not whether the model needs to choose the next tool. The table relates each observed need to a likely design and the evidence needed to justify it.
